bugs: A row edited while its push is in flight keeps sync_started_at set (markSent only clears rows whose updated_at is unchanged), so it isn't ready again until the 15-minute claim expires. The change is resent late but not lost; confirmed with a probe (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:77-82).

synced_at = now() is written after the response arrives, and the check is `updated_at > synced_at` at one-second precision. An edit in the same second right after markSent is never resent (confirmed with a probe).
The optimistic check compares updated_at at one-second precision (toDateTimeString). Two edits within one second during a push are treated as unchanged, and the newer quantity is marked synced.

failed() clears sync_started_at for every id without checking the claim is still its own. If the job runs after its rows were re-claimed (e.g. picked from a backlog after 15 minutes), it releases another job's claim and the next dispatcher run sends those rows twice.

bugs: synced_at is set to the time the rows were read ($startedAt), and the check is `updated_at > synced_at` at one-second precision. An edit in the same second as the read is never resent (confirmed with a probe; the window is about 1 second per job).

failed() clears sync_started_at for every id without checking the claim is still its own. A job that finally fails after its rows were re-claimed releases the other job's claim, which can lead to a duplicate send.

Rows reported missing get disabled_at but also synced_at = $startedAt in the same flow. That is harmless, but the job does two separate updates without a transaction, so a crash in between leaves missing SKUs synced but not disabled (they won't retry unless edited).

v.rationale:
Both suites pass (impl-1: 24 tests; impl-2: 26 tests). I probed edge cases in both with throwaway tests and deleted them afterwards. The two implementations share the same dispatcher design: they claim rows under a lock (lockForUpdate re-check in a transaction), use onOneServer and withoutOverlapping, update with toBase() so updated_at isn't touched, derive retryUntil from the claim TTL, and release the claim in failed(). They also share one flaw: failed() can release a claim that a newer job now holds, which can cause a duplicate send.

The difference is how each handles edits made while a push is in flight. impl-1 uses a check on updated_at compared as a one-second string, grouped per value. It works but is harder to read, and an edited row stays claimed until the 15-minute TTL runs out, so the update is resent late. It also writes synced_at = now() after the response, so an edit in that same second is lost. impl-2 sets synced_at to the time the rows were read, which is simpler and makes in-flight edits ready again right away. Its only loss window is an edit within the same second as the read. impl-2's tests are also more idiomatic: withFakeQueueInteractions/assertReleased instead of Mockery, and time travel for claim abandonment. Overall, impl-2 is simpler and slightly more correct, so it ranks first.
